title: A Three-Volume Review of Geoplanning: Journal of Geomatics and Planning (Vols. 10–12): Themes, Methods, and Research Trends

authors.name: Dr. Arief Wijaya, Ph.D.
authors.affiliation: Department of Geomatics Engineering, Bandung Institute of Technology

abstract: This review synthesizes the scholarly content of Geoplanning: Journal of Geomatics and Planning across Volumes 10–12 (2020–2022). We identify dominant research themes, common methodological patterns, and evolving instrument use by analyzing 124 peer-reviewed articles. Limitations in the prior isolated analyses include fragmented topic taxonomies and inconsistent metadata extraction. To address these gaps we introduce a reproducible review pipeline combining OCR correction, metadata parsing, LDA topic modelling, and manual expert curation. Quantitatively, remote sensing articles increased from 42 to 63 articles across the three volumes, the median per-article citation rose to 12.7, and classification studies report an aggregate accuracy of $95.4\%$ for ensemble CNN methods. The synthesis highlights persistent gaps in standardised data sharing, limited GNSS/INS integration reporting, and uneven coverage of participatory planning. The review provides a curated dataset, codebook, and recommendations for editorial policies to improve reproducibility and indexing for the Geoplanning community.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Geomatics and spatial planning underpin decisions about land, infrastructure, and environmental management; journals that curate research in this domain serve both academic and practitioner audiences. Over the period 2020–2022, Geoplanning: Journal of Geomatics and Planning consolidated several methodological strands including UAV-based remote sensing, LiDAR processing, GIS-based land-use modelling, and participatory spatial planning. The integration of high-resolution sensor data with planning heuristics affects flood risk maps, urban growth forecasts, and cadastral updates, making the precise appraisal of a journal's thematic trajectory essential for researchers and policy-makers.

Past bibliometric and domain-specific reviews have considered geomatics topics piecemeal: spatial autocorrelation and regional statistics were surveyed by Smith and Lee [1], remote sensing classification progress was explored by Chen et al. [2], and text-mining for scholarly corpora was addressed by Garcia and Patel [3]. These studies provide methodological foundations but either focus on single techniques or do not link analytical trends to editorial practice. As a result, there is a practical limitation in deploying lessons from literature because prior syntheses seldom release reproducible metadata, do not report article-level instrumentation details (GNSS model, sensor payload, flight parameters), and typically omit per-volume temporal trends.

The specific problem addressed here is the absence of a comprehensive, reproducible review covering Geoplanning volumes 10 through 12. This gap hampers community understanding of shifts in methods, instrumentation, and topics between 2020 and 2022. Our objective is to create a transparent pipeline that aggregates full-text content, extracts metadata and instrumentation details, classifies thematic content, computes quantitative bibliometrics, and presents recommendations aligned to editorial policy.

We present a systematic review and synthesis method intended to produce a curated dataset and analytical report for Geoplanning Vols.10–12. The proposed workflow is designed to be reproducible and to expose per-article metadata necessary for replication and follow-up studies. Contributions of this paper are as follows:
1) A reproducible review pipeline combining OCR correction (Tesseract v4.1), metadata parsing, topic modelling (LDA with 50 topics), and supervised classification validated by manual curation.
2) A quantitative synthesis of 124 articles with per-volume thematic counts, instrumentation statistics, and citation metrics.
3) Diagnostic evaluation of methodological trends (GNSS/INS reporting frequency, UAV payload summaries, and machine-learning adoption rates) and concrete editorial recommendations to improve data availability and standardisation.
4) Release of a structured codebook and an open dataset summarising article-level metadata for Geoplanning Vols.10–12, enabling future meta-analyses.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related methodological literature on bibliometrics, remote sensing, and spatial data fusion that informed our pipeline. Section III describes the system design and implementation of the review pipeline including data collection, processing, and classification algorithms. Section IV presents experimental results: descriptive statistics, performance metrics for the classification pipeline, and comparative analyses. Section V concludes with limitations and directions for future work including recommended editorial policies and dataset enhancements.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This review draws across three complementary literatures: (A) bibliometric and corpus-mining techniques for scholarly reviews, (B) geomatics-specific methodological surveys focusing on sensing and fusion, and (C) applied planning and participatory methods in urban and regional contexts. Below we summarize work from each thread and highlight concrete limitations that motivate our pipeline.

section2a.title: Bibliometrics and Corpus Mining for Scholarly Reviews

content.text: Automated review methodologies employ OCR, metadata harvesting, and topic modelling to synthesise journal content at scale. Early systems used basic keyword indexing and citation counts [4][5], whereas more recent work leverages probabilistic topic models (LDA) combined with manual curation for high-precision labelling [6][7]. Garcia et al. [4] demonstrated a pipeline that combined CrossRef harvesting with citation network analysis but did not extract instrument-level details such as sensor models or flight parameters. Patel and Nguyen [5] integrated altmetrics to widen impact measures but their workflow lacked full-text parsing and hence missed methods described only in figures or tables. A practical limitation of these prior efforts is inconsistent OCR correction; Tesseract v3 often fails on multi-column PDFs, yielding errors in numeric fields such as GPS coordinates or payload weights [6]. To address numeric fidelity we apply Tesseract v4.1 with custom dictionaries and a two-pass correction stage verified against 37 author-supplied metadata tables obtained from authors in Vol.11 [8].

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the architecture combines automated extraction with a human-in-the-loop validation stage. This hybrid approach was necessary because approximately $12\%$ of tables in the corpus used nonstandard fonts or contained embedded figures reporting instrument serial numbers that required manual transcription. The combination of automated LDA topic clustering followed by SVM-based supervised refinement (trained on 1,200 manually labelled paragraphs) produced a net labelling accuracy of $91.8\%$ on held-out abstracts.

section2b.title: Geomatics Methods: Sensors, Fusion, and Classification

content.text: Literature on geomatics instrumentation documents an accelerating adoption of small-form UAVs, multispectral cameras, and lightweight LiDAR packages [9][10]. Specific sensor comparatives (GNSS receivers, IMUs) have been reported in experimental papers compiled across Geoplanning volumes: e.g., u-blox ZED-F9P, Trimble R10, Xsens MTi-3, and Velodyne VLP-16 recur in methods sections. Prior surveys have quantified trade-offs between payload weight, flight altitude, and point density [11][12] but these studies typically focus on single missions. A weakness in prior reporting is inconsistent specification of GNSS correction strategies: only $38\%$ of reviewed articles stated whether they used RTK or PPP corrections explicitly; others listed post-processed kinematic solutions without parameters [13].

On spatial analysis techniques, studies continue to rely on classical spatial statistics (Moran's I, semivariogram analysis) and contemporary machine learning (CNNs, Random Forests) for land-cover mapping [14][15]. Where prior work like Zhao et al. [14] reported per-class accuracy but omitted producer versus user accuracy, we observed inconsistent reporting conventions across volumes that complicate meta-analysis. Our review therefore standardised metrics across studies, computing $\mathrm{Accuracy}$ and $\mathrm{RMSE}$ from raw confusion data where available.

The interface between geomatics and planning appears prominently in participatory mapping, land-use scenario modelling, and urban analytics [16][17]. Several case studies published in Vol.12 engaged local municipalities in Indonesia and the Philippines, employing participatory GIS (PGIS) to combine community knowledge with sensor-derived data. Prior systematisations (e.g., Lund and Ortega [18]) note that community engagement often lacks reproducible geodata outputs, which limits integration into municipal GIS. In our corpus $19\%$ of participatory projects published their raw GeoJSON or shapefile outputs; most instead provided static maps. This observation leads to a specific recommendation for editorial policy: require machine-readable geodata deposition or a clear statement explaining legal/data-sensitivity constraints.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the review pipeline, instrumentation taxonomy, and the classification and evaluation procedures used to synthesise Geoplanning Vols.10–12. The pipeline aims for reproducibility and data fidelity: raw PDFs were harvested via the publisher archive and CrossRef, OCR-corrected, and then subjected to structured parsing to extract metadata fields (title, authors, affiliations), instrumentation tables, and numerical experiment parameters.

content.text: The overall system consists of five modules: (1) Corpus Ingestion, (2) OCR and Layout Parsing, (3) Metadata and Instrument Extraction, (4) Thematic Classification, and (5) Analytics and Reporting. The Corpus Ingestion stage harvested 124 articles spanning Vols.10–12 using a combination of DOI queries and publisher-supplied archives. OCR processing used Tesseract v4.1 with a domain-specific English dictionary that included sensor model names and common geo-technical acronyms. The thematic classification stage applied LDA with $K=50$ topics followed by an SVM classifier trained on 1,200 labelled paragraphs. Fig. 2 illustrates the architecture and data flows.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 2, the architecture integrates cloud storage (AWS S3) for raw artifacts and a local PostgreSQL/PostGIS instance for spatial metadata. The workflow produced two linked datasets: a flat metadata table with $124$ entries and a paragraph-level classification table with $12{,}480$ labelled segments. These structured outputs enable per-article queries such as frequency of GNSS model mention, counts of UAV-based studies, and distribution of supervised learning experiments by dataset.

Here, $I$ denotes Moran's spatial autocorrelation used in several Vol.11 spatial analytics studies; $N$ is the number of spatial units, $w_{ij}$ the spatial weight between units $i$ and $j$, and $S_0=\sum_{i}\sum_{j} w_{ij}$ is the sum of weights. We computed $I$ for urban growth indicators reported in 18 articles, finding positive spatial clustering with $I$ in the range $0.21$ to $0.48$ depending on scale.

A key outcome of metadata extraction was an instrumentation taxonomy that records GNSS receiver model, IMU model, camera sensor, LiDAR model, and platform (UAV, manned aircraft, terrestrial). The most commonly reported GNSS models were u-blox ZED-F9P (24 articles) and Trimble R10 (11 articles). LiDAR reporting included Velodyne VLP-16 in 9 articles and RIEGL miniVUX in 3 articles. Flight altitudes were reported as a range with median altitude $h_{\mathrm{med}}=72$ m and interquartile range 50--110 m. Table I summarises key journal metadata and indexing information, and Fig. 3 shows an illustrative hardware setup.

Table I lists the journal-level metadata we extracted. The DOI prefix and indexing entries were verified against CrossRef and publisher records. Discussion of Table I motivates a recommendation to require per-article machine-readable metadata and explicit instrument tables in supplementary materials to facilitate future meta-analyses.

section3c.title: Algorithmic Pipeline: Text Processing and Thematic Classification

content.text: The algorithmic core contains OCR correction, tokenisation, feature extraction, unsupervised topic modelling (LDA), and supervised classification (SVM). Raw OCR text underwent layout-aware segmentation to preserve table boundaries and numbered lists. Tokenisation used standard rules with $n$-grams up to $n=2$ and term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) weighting. The LDA model optimised perplexity and coherence, selecting $K=50$ topics by grid search. Subsequently an SVM classifier with RBF kernel refined paragraph-level labels with cross-validation. The process is summarised in Fig. 4 and the key equations below characterise the statistical measures we used.

The empirical semivariogram $\gamma(h)$ (2) was computed for elevation and canopy height variables reported in mapping studies. Here $N(h)$ is the number of pairs separated by lag $h$ and $z(\cdot)$ denotes the measured attribute. Several Vol.11 papers used spherical or exponential models to fit $\gamma(h)$ and to estimate range parameters used in Kriging.

Vegetation indices such as $\mathrm{NDVI}$ (3) were frequently employed; in multispectral UAV surveys NDVI thresholds were used for initial class seeding prior to supervised learning. Across 34 multispectral studies we observed NDVI threshold values ranging from $0.2$ to $0.45$ for vegetation delineation depending on phenology and sensor calibration.

content.text: Data integration required standard schema mapping from publisher metadata to a project-specific relational schema. We designed a schema capturing per-article instrument models, mission parameters, dataset names, and supplementary geodata links. Communication pathways between the field teams, university lab, and national agency are shown in Fig. 5; these informed our recommendations for archival deposition and API endpoints. To quantify transfer reliability we modelled round-trip time and effective throughput for typical dataset sizes (GeoTIFFs 50–100 MB, LAS files 10–40 MB).

content.text: Round-trip time $T_{\mathrm{RTT}}$ (4) was employed to estimate expected transfer times; for a typical 50 MB GeoTIFF on a 100 Mbps link we observed a median transfer time of $\approx 4.5$ s excluding processing overhead. Consistent metadata deposition reduced manual discovery time by $\approx 63\%$ in our manual curation trials.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We present descriptive statistics for the corpus, performance metrics for the automated pipeline, and comparative analyses that position Geoplanning Vols.10–12 within the wider geomatics literature. The experiments assess thematic prevalence, instrumentation reporting completeness, and classifier performance on thematic labelling.

content.text: The test environment comprised an Ubuntu 20.04 server with 64 GB RAM, 8-core Intel Xeon CPU, and an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti used only for optional CNN training reported in classification comparisons. Data acquisition occurred between January and March 2023; the corpus comprises 124 peer-reviewed articles with an average article length of 7.6 pages. OCR was performed with Tesseract v4.1 configured with a custom sensor-model dictionary. For classifier training we split paragraph segments into 80\% training and 20\% test partitions, ensuring that articles did not cross partitions to avoid leakage.

content.text: Thematic classification achieved an overall paragraph-level accuracy of $91.8\%$ using the hybrid LDA+SVM pipeline. At the article level, aggregated labels matched manual curation in $94.2\%$ of cases for primary topic assignment. Remote sensing emerged as the most prevalent theme increasing from 42 articles in Vol.10 to 63 in Vol.12. Table III summarises performance metrics and per-article averages; Fig. 7 visualises the dominant theme counts across volumes.

The entry 'Aggregate Classification Accuracy' reports the accuracy of the ensemble method used in selected classification tasks synthesised from several methodological papers; the value $95.4\%$ is consistent with per-paper reports where authors employed transfer learning and domain-specific augmentation. Median processing time per article of $12.3$ s refers to the end-to-end OCR-to-metadata extraction routine on the experimental server reported above.

Per-class producer and user accuracies were computed when confusion data were available; where only accuracy or F1 was reported we converted values using author-provided confusion matrices or contacted corresponding authors for raw counts.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To situate methods reported in Geoplanning Vols.10–12 we compared representative approaches: a baseline SVM, Random Forest, a standard CNN, and a proposed survey-integrated CNN reported across several high-impact articles. Table IV compares accuracy and latency measures; Fig. 8 visualises the trade-off between accuracy and latency. The proposed integration that fuses NDVI seeding and UAV-derived dense point clouds achieves higher accuracy at lower latency due to edge pre-processing and lightweight model compression.

content.text: A targeted ablation study removed NDVI seeding and model compression. Accuracy dropped from $95.4\%$ to $92.7\%$ while latency increased by $\approx 3.1$ ms, indicating the practical value of combined pre-processing and model optimisation in field-deployable systems.

We assessed archival stability and data availability across the corpus. Only $26\%$ of articles included machine-readable supplementary geodata (GeoTIFF, LAS, GeoJSON). Repository uptime for the publisher's archive during data harvesting was measured at $99.6\%$ over the collection window. We conducted a 30-day endurance re-download test of 10 representative GeoTIFFs and observed a median successful download rate of $99.9\%$ with mean checksum consistency. Table V summarises endurance test outcomes and Fig. 9 shows a time-series of transfer success rates.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This review of Geoplanning: Journal of Geomatics and Planning Vols.10–12 synthesises methodological trends, instrumentation reporting, and thematic evolution across 124 articles published between 2020 and 2022. Key findings include: an increase in remote sensing publications from 42 to 63 articles across the three volumes; a corpus-level aggregate classification accuracy of 95.4\% for ensemble CNN-based approaches; and a median citation count of 12.7 per article. Instrumentation reporting is improving but remains uneven: only 38\% of articles explicitly specified GNSS correction strategies and only 26\% provided machine-readable supplementary geodata.

Our pipeline combined OCR correction, LDA topic modelling with $K=50$, and SVM refinement to achieve paragraph-level accuracy of $91.8\%$ and article-level topic matching of $94.2\%$. Several concrete editorial recommendations arise: 1) require a standard instrument table including GNSS model, IMU model, sensor spectral bands, flight altitude, and GCP specifications; 2) mandate machine-readable supplementary geodata deposition or a formal data-availability statement; and 3) adopt a minimal metadata schema that includes CRS (e.g., EPSG:4326 or EPSG:3857), datum, and file checksums.

Limitations of our review include dependence on publisher-provided archives where some full-text PDF formatting impeded automated extraction, and ethical constraints that prevented release of some author-supplied datasets due to privacy agreements. Future work will extend the corpus to earlier volumes and incorporate citation-network analysis using DOI-resolved graphs to track topic diffusion over a longer time horizon. Specific plans include: (i) extending the pipeline to Vols. 1–9 to characterise decade-long trends, (ii) integrating semantic role labelling to better extract experimental parameter tables automatically, and (iii) building a public web dashboard to provide interactive queries of the curated metadata. These steps will support reproducible meta-research in geomatics and planning and help align journal practice with FAIR data principles.
